podcast.title: Death in 2015
podcast.body: Lemmy of Motörhead died of cancer on December 28, 2015. His death, along with Scott Weiland's earlier in the month, marked a sad start to a period of significant losses in the music world. "Then Lemmy of Motorhead died of cancer on December 28."

podcast.body: Lemmy of Motorhead was among the notable figures who came to pay their respects at the Ramones' final concert on August 6, 1996, in Hollywood. "All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."

podcast.title: Failed Petition for Heavy Metal Element
podcast.body: A petition to name a heavy metal element after Lemmy of Motorhead failed. The primary reasons were that scientific rules for naming new elements do not allow for musicians as sources, only mythological concepts, minerals, places, countries, properties, or scientists. Additionally, the new "heavy" elements (113, 115, 117, 118) are actually classified as non-metals on the periodic table. "This petition was inspired by the idea that an actual heavy metal element be named after Lemmy and with atomic weights between 113 and 118, these new elements are the heaviest yet discovered. Perfect. Awesome. Sounds great. However, if we look at the periodic table, you'll see that these new elements occupy space on the right hand side. This is the area of the table reserved for non-metals."

podcast.title: Marine Worm Species
podcast.body: Lemmy Kilmister of Motorhead has a marine worm named after him, making him one of several musicians honored in this way. "Sepul Turah, the Brazilian heavy metal band, has won as does King Diamond, so does Lemmy from Motorhead."

podcast.title: Rainbow Bar & Grill Tribute
podcast.body: Lemmy Kilmister was a regular patron at The Rainbow Bar & Grill on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles. Following his death, the venue preserved his favorite chair at the end of the bar as a permanent tribute. Patrons can also order "a Lemmy," which is his preferred drink of Jack Daniel's and Coke. "Lemmy of Motorhead was a fixture at a venue called the Rainbow in Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles. After he died, they preserved his favorite chair at the end of the bar as a tribute. You can also order a drink in the bar called a Lemmy, which is favorite drink, Jack Daniels and Coke."

podcast.title: Roadie for Jimi Hendrix
podcast.body: Before becoming a performer with Motorhead, Lemmy Kilmister worked as a roadie for Jimi Hendrix, where he was responsible for "humping gear." This personal experience gave him a unique understanding and sympathy for road crews. "Lemmy is uniquely sympathetic to road crews because he himself used to hump gear for Jimmy Hendrix before he moved on to performing."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."

xref.title: Axis Memorabilia Collection
xref.body: During his lifetime, Lemmy Kilmister was known for his collection of memorabilia from Axis countries of World War II, which included items from Germany, Hungary, and Italy. "he collected material from all the Axis countries of World War II. So Germany, yes, but also Hungary, Italy, and so on."

xref.title: Exile to England
xref.body: Following a violent confrontation related to his drug activities and a brush with the law, Dillon's parents gave him an ultimatum to leave Kingston, which he signed an agreement not to return to for several years. He traveled to England, his first time on a plane or subway, where he busked, squatted, and famously drank with Lemmy from Motörhead, resolving to pursue music instead of a life of crime. "So I got on a plane. I went to England, never been on a plane in my life, never been on a subway."

xref.title: Flamboyance and Influence
xref.body: Despite performing as a Black and gay artist in the US South in the 1950s, Little Richard's flamboyance, energy, and music had a massive effect across rock and roll. His influence extended to artists like The Beatles, James Brown, David Bowie, and even Lemmy of Motorhead, reverberating through the entire genre. "His flamboyance, his energy, and his music reverberated through all of rock and roll."

xref.title: Origin of "Headbanging" Term
xref.body: According to Lemmy, the term "headbanging" was derived from the name of his band, suggesting a direct link such as "Motörhead banging." The band's fast songs, some reaching 200 beats per minute, put extreme strain on the neck. "Then if you had talked to Lemmy, he would say that the term head banging was derived from the name of his band."
